source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving, Exp 3 (full text re-read)
finding: Exp 3 separates the two mechanisms in solution rates, but the Type D time gain after tautology exposure has a simple alternative cause. The tautological set contained one tautological Type D item. That item still needs chunk decomposition, so the later Type D gain can be plain practice at decomposing.
numbers: N=34 (regular-first 18, tautology-first 16). Type C Block 1: regular 61% vs tautological 100% (chi2(1,34)=12.59, p<.001). Regular-first Type C Block 2: 100% (chi2=13.85, p<.001). Type D Block 1: 61% vs 69% (chi2=0.22, p=.64); Block 2: 92% vs 94%; Block1-to-2 gain in regular-first chi2(1,18)=5.79 p<.05, in tautology-first chi2(1,16)=3.28 p=.07. Type D solution time, Block 1 regular-first vs Block 2 tautology-first: U=65, Z=2.71, p<.01. Type C same comparison: U=8, Z=4.67, p<.001. Type A: U=128, p=.59. Tautological D vs regular D on first encounter: U=116, p=.33. Set sizes: regular set 6 items (2 A, 2 B, 1 C, 1 D); tautological set 4 items (2 A, 1 C, 1 D).
quote: tautological form does not affect initial difficulty and transfer in problems of Type D.
limits: The set composition is read from the Method section; the practice explanation is my inference, not stated by the authors. One task family, one lab, small N, one D item per set.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping O4 and O6 as separate operators. The Type D time gain is not evidence that relaxing a constraint also loosens a chunk. Closes the doubt in gap 5 for the solution-time result, but does not test cueing.

source: Knoblich et al. (1999) Table 13 and General Discussion (full text re-read)
finding: Across Exp 1A, 1B and 2 the predicted difficulty order A<B<C held in solution times every time; in solution frequencies some A-B and A-D contrasts were not significant, which the authors blame on ceiling effects. The difficulty gap vanished on a second encounter in all four experiments.
numbers: Exp 1A solution frequency A>D p=.13 (not significant; confirms the earlier correction to a04). Over 75% of Type B solved in Exp 1B and over 80% in Exp 2 (ceiling). Exp 3: tautological Type A was solved more slowly than regular Type A (U=34, Z=-1.17, p=.09), explained post hoc.
quote: The effect of task difficulty observed on a first encounter always disappeared when the same problem types were encountered a second time.
limits: Authors' own summary of their own data. Tightness (A vs D) is the weaker half of the theory in frequencies.
agent_relevance: Difficulty gaps shrink after one exposure, so a per-item test of O4/O6 must use fresh items, and a long shared context can wash out the effect of a cue.

source: Miller, Wiley, Ohlsson (2025) Testing the independence of representational change theory processes, Thinking & Reasoning
finding: Full abstract read (earlier b22 was a shortened version). Cuing chunk decomposition (CD) helped only CD problems; cuing constraint relaxation (CR) helped only CR problems. Both cues together did no better than one and sometimes lowered solving. Study 2: CD instructions spread somewhat to CD solutions that did not match the instruction; CR instructions did not raise CR solutions; single cues sometimes lowered solving on other problems.
numbers: Authors identified through Crossref and Semantic Scholar metadata: Taylor Strickland Miller, Jennifer Wiley, Stellan Ohlsson. Sample sizes, effect sizes and instruction wording are NOT available: the full text returned HTTP 403 and no open copy was found.
quote: A combined instruction condition did not outperform the single instruction conditions, and in some cases decreased solution rates.
limits: Abstract only for the numbers. Human matchstick arithmetic only. The abstract says CR cues failed to help in Study 2, so the CR effect is weak.
agent_relevance: Supports routing to ONE operator per impasse. A router that fires O4 and O6 together is not supported, and may hurt. Still no LLM test.

source: Xing, Zhang, Sun, Zhang, Wang (2013) The mechanism of constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition and the related prototype elicitation effect in logogriph tasks, Acta Psychologica Sinica 45(10)
finding: In Chinese word-riddle tasks, hinting with a prototype (an example that shows the needed move) helped constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition more than a non-prototype hint or no hint. Seen as a search-result summary only.
numbers: No numbers seen. The publisher server refused the PDF fetch.
limits: Search snippet only. Different task family (logogriphs) and language. Compares hint types, not named-mechanism vs generic cue.
agent_relevance: An example that shows the move (a worked case of dropping a constraint) may beat a bare instruction. This is a lead for the cue design test, not evidence.

source: Danek, Wiley, Oellinger (2016) Solving classical insight problems without Aha! experience: 9 dot, 8 coin and matchstick arithmetic problems, J. Problem Solving 9(1)
finding: The Aha rating falls as more constraints must be relaxed. Many people solved these classic problems without any Aha. So a solved insight item is not proof of a sudden re-representation.
numbers: Abstract page only: the prediction that Aha likelihood decreases with the number of constraints to relax was supported. Exact rates are in the PDF, which I could not open.
quote: the likelihood of experiencing an Aha! would decrease with increasing numbers of constraints that must be relaxed.
limits: Abstract only. Self-report. Links to gap 9: the suddenness story is weaker for multi-constraint items.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a sudden answer change in a trace as the signature of the right operator. Deeper constraint stacks produce gradual, multi-step change.

source: Ohlsson (2011) Deep Learning: How the Mind Overrides Experience, ch. 4 Creative insight: the redistribution theory (publisher page)
finding: Only the chapter opening is public. It states a Raisins in the Dough principle: a creative project needs several short insights spread through mostly analytical work. It sets three tasks: describe analytical thinking, explain what happens in insight, and explain how insight extends analytical thinking. The redistribution steps are not visible.
limits: Full chapter paywalled. The activation-redistribution mechanism (a21) therefore remains unverified at the text level. A search summary of the book's front matter lists redistribution of activation as one of three principles.
agent_relevance: Operational reading stays a hypothesis: after an impasse, change which knowledge is active rather than add more search. Nothing here yet tells us how to use it for LLM memory retrieval.

source: MathSticks (2025) A benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles, arXiv 2510.00483 (HTML read)
finding: Strong reasoning models do far better when the equation is given as text than as an image, and do worse when the operator sign must change. The paper claims a bias toward digit edits but gives no count by edit type.
numbers: 1,411,388 puzzles (43.12% single-solution). Text average accuracy: o3 60.00, Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25, Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50, o4-mini 24.75, Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50, Claude Sonnet 4 2.25, GPT-4o 0. Visual: o3 38.50, Gemini-2.5-Pro 22.50. Human 91.72 (+/-6.13). By level (text, o3): L1 73, L2 56, L3 56, L4 55. Sign-changed vs no-sign-change (text/visual): o3 51.45/34.20 vs 65.19/41.22; Gemini-2.5-Pro 38.91/19.70 vs 49.09/25.05; o4-mini 21.15/10.54 vs 26.95/9.88. 1-move vs 2-move (text, o3): 82.50 vs 52.88.
limits: Generated puzzles, not Knoblich's A-D types. Sign-changed is only a proxy for operator edits (Type B/C-like). No tightness labels, no prompt ablation, no chain-of-thought test, error categories reported without counts.
agent_relevance: First per-class hint for gap 3: operator-change items are 8 to 14 points harder in text for the three strongest models. This fits the constraint-depth ladder (value moves easiest). It is not yet a test of A-D or of tightness.

source: Shin and Kaneko (2024) Large language models lack understanding of character composition of words, arXiv 2405.11357 (PDF text read)
finding: Models treat a word as a token unit and fail at simple sub-word edits that humans do perfectly. Whole-word replacement is easy; insertion, deletion and counting are weak. So what is a tight chunk depends on the tokenizer.
numbers: Character-level F-scores (human / GPT-4 / Claude / Gemini / Mistral): insertion 1.0/.368/.268/.272/.436; deletion 1.0/.277/.403/.302/.357; replacement .971/.558/.567/.771/.392; word retrieval .994/.595/.461/.574/.641. 100 prompts per task. Character counting accuracy for GPT-4 was .59 in the table I read.
limits: Not an insight study. Models are 2024 vintage. Failures involving numeric positions appear at token level too, so tokenization is not the only cause (the authors say so).
agent_relevance: For chunk-decomposition items (O6) the unit to split should be handed to the model in a form it can edit, by code (spell out characters, list digits). Tight for a person is not tight for a model.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation, arXiv 2505.06120 (PDF text read)
finding: After a wrong early turn, models seldom recover. They make assumptions early, produce a premature answer, then over-rely on it. Giving the whole instruction in one clean prompt (concat) keeps most performance; recap or snowball restores only part.
numbers: Average drop single-turn to multi-turn 39% over six tasks (200,000+ simulated conversations). Aptitude loss -15%, unreliability +112%. Snowball mitigates the full-to-sharded drop by 15 to 20% only (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, four tasks).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover.
limits: Underspecified-instruction tasks, not insight items. The failed content is the model's own early answer, which is the closest analogue found to a carried-over failed frame.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 6: a failed frame kept in context lowers later success. Restating the problem in a fresh context beats stacking more turns. This favours a clean-context re-attempt as the default for O4/O6, with the failed attempt summarised in code, not left in the text. Not yet tested on insight items.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot in LLMs, arXiv 2507.02778 v3, COLM 2026 (PDF text read)
finding: The same error is corrected when it appears as the user's text but not when it appears as the model's own earlier output. Appending the single word Wait removes most of the gap, and lets a non-reasoning model nearly match its reasoning sibling.
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: blind spot averages 64.5%. Appending Wait cuts it by 89.3% and raises mean accuracy by 156%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Table 3 macro accuracy base / +Wait / reasoning: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567/0.902/0.908; phi-4 0.325/0.701/0.707; Qwen3-14B non-thinking 0.117/0.868/0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045/0.793/0.894.
limits: Errors are injected, not natural. Open-source non-reasoning models only. Math-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Two uses. (1) A model keeps its own earlier frame (gap 6). (2) A correction marker is a cheap generic cue, so the baseline for gap 1 must include a Wait-style cue as well as a named-constraint cue. Presenting the failed attempt as a user-supplied draft to critique, not as the model's own output, is a testable trick.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs, arXiv 2501.18585 (HTML read)
finding: Wrong answers contain far more switches between lines of thought. Most wrong responses already contain a correct thought. A decoding penalty on switching adds a little accuracy on hard sets.
numbers: Incorrect responses show 418% more thought switching and use 225% more tokens than correct ones (averaged over o1-like models). More than 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought; in over half of those, more than 10% of thoughts are correct. TIP Pass@1: AIME24 QwQ-32B-Preview 38.3 to 44.1 (+5.8), R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1, DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8; GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7.
limits: Math and science, not insight items. The paper's own tables disagree on the QwQ AIME24 baseline (46.7 vs 38.3) and the text does not explain it. Switching is a failure of depth, the opposite pattern to a fixation impasse (too little change), so it does not detect fixation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a visible output signal (thought-switch rate) separates wrong from right, but it flags scatter, not fixation. Gap 4: generation is often fine (over 70% of wrong answers hold a correct thought), so selection by code (G5) should be tried before any representation operator.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification, arXiv 2504.05419 (PDF text read)
finding: Hidden states of reasoning models carry whether an intermediate answer is correct, even before it is fully written. A simple probe stops reasoning early without losing accuracy. The model does not use this signal itself.
numbers: In-distribution probes: ROC-AUC above 0.7, ECE below 0.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B over 0.9 AUC on AIME. Probe-based early exit cut tokens by about 24% with no accuracy loss.
limits: Needs hidden-state access, so it does not fit a black-box scaffold. Probes trained per dataset; out-of-distribution transfer weaker on AIME. Math and logic only.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that endorsement, not generation, is often the broken step (gap 4). The usable part for us is the design idea: gate on a calibrated correctness score. Without weights, use verbalised confidence or code checks, which are weaker.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Efficiently serving LLM reasoning programs with Certaindex, arXiv 2412.20993 (abstract page read)
finding: Intermediate answers often stop changing partway through a long reasoning run. A stability metric over the intermediate answers (certaindex) tells when more compute will not change the answer, and was used for early exit and budget allocation.
numbers: Up to 50% compute saved and 3.3x higher throughput on real workloads with no accuracy drop (abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Built for stopping, not for finding fixation. Does not say how often a stable wrong answer occurs.
agent_relevance: A black-box impasse signal for gap 2: repeated identical candidate answers across resamples or turns. But stable-and-wrong is exactly the fixation case, so stability can only say no news; a separate code check must say wrong. This matches G1: gate on a code-visible failure.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf), arXiv 2508.15260 (abstract page read)
finding: Token-level confidence inside a trace filters out low-quality reasoning traces during or after generation, and beats plain majority voting at much lower token cost.
numbers: Up to 99.9% accuracy on AIME 2025 with DeepConf@512; generated tokens reduced by up to 84.7% vs full parallel thinking (abstract). Models: Qwen3 and GPT-OSS families.
limits: Abstract only. Needs token probabilities. Math benchmarks. Filters traces for voting, not for choosing a reframe.
agent_relevance: Output-derived confidence is a usable gate on sampled attempts when logprobs exist. No evidence it separates fixation from ordinary uncertainty on insight items.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight, appendix details (HTML, first 200k characters read)
finding: Higher first-pass entropy goes with larger gains from the reconsideration cue. The paper tried three cue wordings, and measures spontaneous shifts with a judged pipeline. I found no neutral-resample or named-constraint control in the part I could read.
numbers: Entropy-gated reconsideration: Math +8.41 pp (32.21 to 40.62), crosswords +0.45, Rush Hour +0.01. Cue C1 'Hold on, this reasoning might be wrong. Let's go back and check each step carefully': entropy standardized coefficient 0.79; odds ratio 2.21 per 1 SD (table row alignment uncertain), on 8 x 500 Math items, Qwen2.5-1.5B, T=0.1. Spontaneous-shift detector: GPT-4o judge with lexical prefilter, kappa about 0.726 across prompt variants and 0.79 vs human majority; shift rate 6.31% pooled, 7.6% for Qwen2.5-1.5B.
limits: Stratum tables (C.4 Table 29, D.7 Table 25) and token costs were in the unread final 50k characters. Small models. All cue wordings are generic.
agent_relevance: Entropy of the first pass is the one output signal with a measured link to cue benefit (gap 2). It needs logprobs. All three cues are generic, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Xu et al. (2023, rev. 2024) LLMs and the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus: successes, failures and the importance of object-based representations, arXiv 2305.18354 (abstract page read)
finding: Giving GPT-4 an object-based version of the grid, produced by an external tool, nearly doubled solved ARC tasks and gave near-perfect scores on a 1D version. Failures came from how objects were encoded as text.
numbers: GPT-4 solved 13 of 50 easiest ARC tasks with text grids. The external object-based representation nearly doubled the number solved. Near-perfect on 1D-ARC.
limits: Abstract only (the PDF download failed). The representation change is done by a code tool and may use hand-tuned object extraction.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 7: on an ARC-type target, re-representing the input by code (O6-like) pays off, while asking the model to reframe is not shown to. Order the operators: code-side re-encoding first, model-side reframe second.

source: Gap search log: arXiv listing scans for named-versus-generic cues (this session)
finding: I scanned arXiv listings for insight problems, matchsticks, impasse detection, fixation and hint levels. No paper compares a named-constraint or named-unit cue with a generic reconsider cue on LLM insight items. Hint-level work exists only for RL training (StepHint, SEELE), faulty-premise hints (FaultyMath, abstract has no hint numbers) and benchmark prompt variants (Ko-MuSR, Automated LLM Speedrunning).
numbers: 43-result hint listing: 0 head-to-head general-vs-specific tests. Title search 'insight problem solving LLM' returned 1 irrelevant paper. 'matchstick puzzles' returned MathSticks 2510.00483 and one EEG study. Searches for impasse and stuck-loop detection returned nothing. arXiv keyword matching is weak, so a miss is not proof of absence.
limits: Negative search, done after the web-search quota ran out. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, so coverage is thinner than it should be.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open and has to be tested in house. The nearest direct hint-specificity result is the human study d03.

source: M-ARC (Feb 2025, arXiv 2502.04381) and follow-up on stronger reasoning models (Jan 2026, arXiv 2601.11866)
finding: Clinical problems built to trigger the Einstellung effect (a learned pattern that no longer fits) beat most 2025 models. By January 2026 the strongest reasoning models reached human-level on the same set, which suggests that fixation on learned patterns shrinks with model strength.
numbers: M-ARC (PDF text read): most LLMs under 50% accuracy, several near or below 20% chance; best Gemini 1.5 Pro 50%, o1 48%; five physicians averaged 66% (SE 5.3%). Follow-up (abstract only): top 5 reasoning models answered 55% to 70% of the questions physicians miss most often, correctly and with high confidence.
limits: Medical QA, not insight puzzles. Follow-up is abstract only with no baseline numbers. Different models between the two papers.
agent_relevance: Fixation effects are model dependent and move fast. Measure on the model we actually use, per task class (gap 7), and do not carry a 2024 conclusion forward.

source: Candidate second datasets found by Crossref lookup: Tseng, Chen, Chen (2014) Thinking Skills and Creativity; Kershaw et al. (2010, 2011) matchstick conference datasets
finding: A 2014 eye-movement study of matchstick arithmetic tests the Dual Factors theory, and two Kershaw et al. conference items test negative transfer and prior-knowledge activation in matchstick arithmetic. Titles and venues only. These are the first places to look for a second dataset on the late sudden shift to the critical element.
numbers: No numbers. Publisher pages blocked (403) and abstract APIs rate-limited.
limits: Titles only. I cannot say whether they replicate the Graf et al. change-point result.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Do not set S6 handling on a single N=61 reanalysis.
